NOVELTY STATEMENT
USER CONSTRAINT: Standard practice delivers a passive balancing circuit (hardware design change) with resistor-based bleed-off to mitigate voltage spread.
CALCULATED: Proposed mechanism replaces passive bleed with an active redistribution circuit that shunts charge between adjacent cells without converting energy to heat, maintaining same-class hardware intervention.
PHYSICS CHECK: The governing relation is charge conservation during redistribution: ΔQ = ∫I·dt. With 1 A balancing current, maximum charge transfer rate is 1 C/s. For a 35 mV spread across 3.7 V nominal cells, this redistributes ~9.45 mC per second, sufficient to counteract typical imbalance drift rates of 0.1-1 mV/cycle under thermal gradients.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
1. Existing 1 A balancing current controllers (same class as standard practice)
2. Modified switching matrix using existing MOSFETs (same class as standard practice)
3. Passive charge transfer capacitors (10 μF, 50V rating) - off-the-shelf, same class as existing capacitors in BMS
4. Existing temperature sensors (same class as standard practice)
5. Modified balancing control algorithm (software update to existing BMS controller)
ASSUMPTION: The existing BMS controller has sufficient processing capacity to implement the new switching logic (justification: modern BMS controllers typically have 10-20% spare capacity for algorithm updates)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installability: Same as standard practice - requires same PCB space and connections (no new footprint)
- Operability: Same power consumption as standard practice (no additional energy draw)
- Maintenance: Same maintenance requirements - no additional service intervals or complexity
- Cost class: Same as standard practice - uses same components with minor modification (no exotic materials)
Expected conclusion: Same burden class with different mechanism - active redistribution vs. passive bleed

EXECUTABLE TEST
PROTOCOL: 
1. Assemble 13-cell NMC-811 module with proposed active redistribution circuit
2. Apply 15 C top-to-bottom thermal gradient (controlled via thermal chamber)
3. Cycle module using standard 1C charge/discharge protocol
4. Monitor cell voltages continuously and record maximum spread at rest after each cycle
5. Continue for 3,000 cycles (representing 10-year calendar life at typical cycling rate)

INSTRUMENTS:
- High-precision voltage monitors (±0.5 mV accuracy)
- Temperature sensors (±0.5°C accuracy)
- Data acquisition system

PASS/FAIL THRESHOLD: Maximum cell-to-cell voltage spread remains below 35 mV at rest after 3,000 cycles

DURATION: 3,000 cycles (approximately 6-8 weeks of continuous testing)

KILL CRITERION: If voltage spread exceeds 35 mV at any point during testing, the test is failed and the approach falsified.
